1:
The book turns from building to guarding, and the witnesses open the chapter on the completed wall and the watch set over it. The reformed John Gill marks the sequence of the work: the wall was now built and the doors set up in the gates, which had not been done when Sanballat sent his earlier letter, so that only now was the fortification of Jerusalem complete. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the whole plan of what follows. The wall being finished (compare Nehemiah 6:15), Nehemiah first secured the city against hostile attack, then took measures to increase its inhabitants, and finally set domestic and civil life in order by the law; here at the outset it is the watching of the walls and gates that is provided for. According to ancient appointment, they add, it fell to the doorkeepers to keep watch over the house of God, and that charge is now extended to the guarding of the city itself, the gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites being entrusted with the care.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears behind the arrangement the word of God to his church, 'I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem' (Isaiah 62:6); for dead walls, without living watchmen, are but a poor defence to a city. Nehemiah appointed the porters, singers, and Levites in their places to their work, which was to attend the temple service, so long neglected and now revived. God's worship, Henry insists, is the defence of a place, and his ministers, when they mind their duty, are watchmen on the walls; the singers and porters set to guard the gates preach that the safety of the city and the service of the sanctuary are one care, not two.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the verse at the head of the chapter's whole business: Nehemiah uses proper precautions in guarding the city gates, then proposes to reckon the people by their genealogies, and so recovers the register of those who came up from Babylon. The witnesses do not divide. They read the setting-up of the doors and the appointing of the watch as the seal upon the finished wall, and as the point at which Nehemiah, having secured the place, could turn to the deeper work of filling it with people. Yet Henry keeps the theology uppermost: walls and watchmen are nothing unless the Lord himself keep the city, for 'except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain' (Psalm 127:1), and it was under that conviction that the guard was set.
2:
The guard of the city is committed to two men, and the witnesses weigh both their office and their character. The reformed John Gill identifies the first, Hanani, as Nehemiah's own brother, the very man who had first brought him the melancholy account of the ruined state of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 1:2); the second, Hananiah, was ruler of the palace or castle. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the wording, noting that the written form of the verb is a clerical slip for the read form, so that the sense is 'I gave charge,' and that the two were set over Jerusalem with the duty of ordering the watch, some of the inhabitants to be at their watch-posts and others before their own houses.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the appointment against Nehemiah's coming absence: it is supposed that the governor was now about to return to the Persian court, and so he committed the city to a man he could trust. He finds in Hananiah two qualifications that make a governor. He was a faithful man, one who had a proper belief in God's government and protection and was devoted to his people's good; and he feared God above many, being the most religious in the congregation, one who would govern by the laws, take no bribes, and abuse no authority, but act in all things with the fear of God before his eyes.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the same portrait into a rule of trust. He that has approved himself faithful in less shall be entrusted with more; and of Hananiah it is said that he feared God above many, for among those who fear God truly there are some who fear him greatly and excel others in the instances of that fear, worthy of the double honour due to such as fear the Lord (Psalm 15:4). Those that fear God, Henry adds, must evidence it by being faithful to all men and universally conscientious; and God's Jerusalem is likely to flourish when those rule in it who excel in virtue and are eminent both for godliness and honesty. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the safety of the restored city was laid not merely on gates and bars but on the integrity of the men set over them, and that Nehemiah, when he could not act himself, was careful whom he deputed, choosing for the charge of the holy city a brother of tried affection and a ruler who feared God above his fellows.
3:
The first order of the new watch concerns the gates, and the witnesses explain both the caution and the custom behind it. The reformed John Gill takes 'until the sun be hot' to mean the heat of the day, or near noon, or at least that the sun should be well up and shining clearly before the gates were opened; the purpose being that if any enemies lay near or in wait they might be discovered by daylight, and the inhabitants be up and ready to defend themselves. The gates that let in trade must not let in a surprise.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the eastern practice that lies behind the command. The meaning, he says, is that the gates were not to be opened before sunrise and were always to be shut at sunset; and this remains the custom to the present day in many cities of the East, where a traveller who arrives after sunset finds the gates shut and, on no consideration, will they be opened till morning, so that the late-comer must lodge in the plain or under the walls. On the last clause he is equally plain: every one was obliged to guard that part of the wall which was opposite his own dwelling, each man set to watch over against his house.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees on both points, glossing 'until the sun be hot' as till it be clear and broad day, when the people will be ready in case of an assault, and taking those who stand by and shut the doors to be the watches appointed to that end. He adds the circumstance the others imply, that Nehemiah was now about to return to the court, and left the charge of the city to these officers in his absence, so that the standing orders about the gates would keep the place secure when its builder was away. The witnesses do not divide. They read the rule as the prudence of a wise governor who trusted neither the darkness nor the carelessness of men: the gates barred while the watch still stood by, opened only in the clear light when danger could be seen, and every citizen made a sentinel over the stretch of wall before his own door. The public safety, they agree, was made to rest on every man's particular care for his own house and his own post, so that the guarding of the city was shared among all who dwelt in it.
4:
Between the great wall just finished and the thin population within it lies a tension the witnesses feel at once. The reformed John Gill dwells first on the compass of the city, its wall built again on the old foundation and enclosing as much ground as ever; he cites the heathen writer Hecataeus, who made the circuit of Jerusalem fifty furlongs, and Josephus, who reckoned it at thirty-three, something over six miles about. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the phrase 'broad on both sides,' the city spacious measured from its centre to the right hand and the left; and they are careful with the closing clause. It does not say there were no houses at all, for the place had been re-inhabited for some ninety years, but only that houses had not been built in proportion to the size of the city, so that much open space still lay waiting to be filled.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the disproportion into an act of faith. Nehemiah, he says, walled the city so as to make room for a people not yet come, with an eye to the promise God had lately made by the prophet, that Jerusalem should yet be replenished (Zechariah 8:3); though the people were now few, he believed they would be multiplied, and therefore built the walls large. Had he not depended on that promise, Henry observes, he might have thought walls without a city as great a reproach as a city without walls; but faith looks to what a place shall be, not only to what it is.

The witnesses read the verse, then, as the seed of the whole project that follows. The very emptiness that might have discouraged became the reason for Nehemiah's next design, to gather and enrol the people and so to increase the dwellers in Jerusalem, a purpose the book will carry forward when lots are cast to bring one in ten into the city (Nehemiah 11:1). Keil and Delitzsch make this the hinge: the spaciousness of the city and the fewness of its people together prompted the measures for its peopling. The great walls were not raised over a desolation to mock it, but thrown wide in hope, a frame prepared against the day when the returning nation should grow to fill them; and the witnesses hear in the plain notice of an under-populated city the quiet confidence of men who built for a future they trusted God to give.
5:
The great enrolment that fills the rest of the chapter springs, the witnesses agree, from a motion of God in Nehemiah's heart. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain that God inspired him with the resolution (as at Nehemiah 2:12) to gather the nobles, the rulers, and the people that they might be reckoned by genealogy, and so to lay a basis for increasing the inhabitants of Jerusalem. While this resolve was under consideration, they add, he found the genealogical register of those who came up at the first, that is, with Zerubbabel and Joshua under Cyrus, and not later with Ezra; and the list he found, which the chapter now transcribes, is identical with the roll preserved in Ezra 2.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on Nehemiah's own confession, 'my God put it into my heart.' Whatever good motion is in our minds, prudent or pious, he says, we must acknowledge it to come from God, for every good gift and every good work are from above; he gives knowledge, he gives grace, all is of him, and therefore all must be to him. What is done by human prudence must be ascribed to the direction of divine Providence, for he that teaches the husbandman his discretion (Isaiah 28:26) teaches the statesman his. Henry knew, too, why the design was needed: the safety of a city depends more upon the number and valour of its inhabitants than upon the height of its walls, and Nehemiah, seeing how few dwelt in Jerusalem, sought to find what families had once belonged there that they might be brought back.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses strike the same note. Adam Clarke observes that with this good man every good thing was of God: if he purposed any good it was because God put it into his heart, and thus in all his ways he acknowledged God, who directed all his steps; John Wesley repeats that whatever good motion is in our minds we must acknowledge to come from God. The reformed John Gill adds that Nehemiah always ascribed to God every good thought that was conducive to the welfare of Jerusalem. So the witnesses make this verse the spiritual hinge of the register. The long catalogue that follows is not the fruit of mere administrative zeal but of a purpose God breathed into his servant; and Henry finds in the very repetition of the old roll a token that the God who put the design in Nehemiah's heart delights to number his people, knowing those that are his and preserving their names in the record of the return.
6:
The register proper opens with its title, 'the children of the province that went up out of the captivity,' and the witnesses read it as the same document, with the same heading, that stands in Ezra 2. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch say plainly that the list here, running to the end of the muster, is identical with that roll: these are the children of the province whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away, now come again to Jerusalem and to Judah, every one to his own city. The reformed John Gill grants the identity but attends to the small differences of number and name that run between the two copies, and offers a reason peculiarly his own. The list in Ezra, he suggests, was made in Babylon, when upon the edict of Cyrus the Jews who meant to go up gave in their names and were registered; but this list was made when they had come to Jerusalem. Between the one taking and the other, some who had enrolled changed their minds and stayed behind, and some died by the way, which makes the numbers fewer here; while others who had not enrolled at first, better disposed toward their country, followed after and swelled the count where it is greater.

Here the witnesses divide over the cause of the divergences, though the disagreement is friendly and the substance never in doubt. Gill traces them to the two occasions of the reckoning, one in Babylon and one at Jerusalem. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley refers them rather to the different names borne by the same persons and to the changes that befell the families in the many years between the first making of the catalogue and its renewal. Adam Clarke keeps to his reconciliation of three copies, that this roll, the roll of Ezra, and the apocryphal Esdras correct one another, the surplus of one supplying the shortfall of another. Keil and Delitzsch, with the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, take many of the differences for the ordinary slips of documents long copied by hand.

Beneath the arithmetic the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the theology in view. The repetition of the roll, he says, intimates the delight the great God takes in the persons and families of his spiritual Israel, and the particular notice he takes of them; he knows those that are his, knows them by name, and has his eye on the register of the children of the captivity. The witnesses thus make the bare title at once a matter for the textual critic and a comfort for the believer: a document to be weighed copy against copy, and a proof that no name of the returning people fell out of the memory of God.
70:
The register turns from people and beasts to the gifts brought for the work, and the reformed John Gill notes that some of the chief of the fathers gave toward the building of the city and the temple, and toward its service. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the figure of the giver here named, the Tirshatha, whose gift heads the offering; and he observes that the Greek of the Codex Alexandrinus reads that the people gave to the Athersatha for the treasure, referring the reader for the meaning of that title to the note at Ezra 2:63, where the Tirshatha is taken for the governor of the returning Jews. The gift set at the head of the list, a thousand drams of gold with basons and priestly garments, is the governor's own, the leader giving first and the people after him.

Here the witnesses raise a question of some nicety, whether this account of the offerings is the very same as that in the parallel at Ezra 2:68. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks that the two differ much: here the Tirshatha, the chief governor, begins the offering, where in the other place he is not mentioned; and the single sum named there exceeds all those here put together. Yet Henry judges it probable that it was the same contribution, the one historian following one copy of the lists and the other another, so that the difference is of the record and not of the deed. He will not build doctrine on the discrepancy: blessed be God, he says, that our faith and hope are not built on the niceties of names and numbers, but on the great things of the law and gospel.

The witnesses read the verse, then, as the beginning of a liberal and orderly offering, led by the governor and followed by the heads of houses, toward the rebuilding of the house of God. Whatever is given to that work, Henry adds, God is not unrighteous to forget; nor shall even a cup of cold water wherewith he is honoured go without its reward. The Tirshatha's gift of gold and basons and garments for the priests, set first in the account, is the token of a people whose leaders put the honour of God's house before their own ease, and whose freewill offerings, small or great, were weighed in heaven by the love that brought them rather than by the tale of the coins.
71:
And some of the chief of the fathers gave to the treasure of the work twenty thousand drams of gold and two thousand and two hundred pound of silver: a second offering, and the reformed John Gill explains its use, that it was put into the treasure out of which the expenses of the temple and its service were to be defrayed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke checks the silver against the versions, noting that the Septuagint reads two thousand three hundred minae, a small difference of the copies in a large sum; and he had elsewhere reckoned such gifts of darics and manehs into many thousands of pounds of English money, the mercy of God appearing in that a people carried away with nothing came home able to give so much.

The grammatical-historical witnesses weigh the figures with more caution. Keil and Delitzsch give the gold of the whole offering as worth many thousands but judge that the account is more exactly rendered in the parallel of Ezra 2:69; Charles Ellicott is franker still, holding Nehemiah's own statement the more correct and supposing that certain of the round numbers in the sister roll have suffered in copying. The two accounts of the same gifts, taken side by side, are among the places where the witnesses prefer Nehemiah's reckoning as the plainer and less corrupted.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the sum from the counting-house to the altar. These offerings, he grants, were nothing compared with the offerings of the princes in David's day, who gave by talents where these gave but by drams; yet these drams, being according to the people's ability, were as acceptable to God as those talents, like the widow's two mites cast into the treasury. The witnesses thus hold together the large sum and the humble means. Measured against the wealth of the first temple the gift was slender, a returning and impoverished people giving in coins where their fathers had given in talents; measured by their means it was liberal, God having so prospered them in exile that they came home able to build; and measured by the heart, which Henry makes the true reckoning, it was full. The twenty thousand drams laid up in the treasure of the work were the freewill gift of men who put the rebuilding of God's house before their own resettlement, and the witnesses honour the offering not for its amount but for the devotion that brought it to the ruined place of the altar.
72:
And that which the rest of the people gave was twenty thousand drams of gold, and two thousand pound of silver, and threescore and seven priests' garments: the offering of the whole congregation, added to the gifts of the governor and the chief fathers. The reformed John Gill reckons the gold at twenty thousand drachms, worth, he says, as many pounds of our money and somewhat more, a considerable sum from a people newly come off a long march and beginning the world anew. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps before the reader why these gifts differ from the like account in the parallel at Ezra 2:69: the Tirshatha being here concerned, and this being another and later collection than the first, it is no wonder that the numbers of the monies and the other things contributed should differ from those set down there.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the worth of the common people's gift. It was given, he observes, not by talents, as the princes gave in David's day when the first temple was preparing (1 Chronicles 29:7), but by drams, the smaller coin of a poorer age; yet these drams, being according to their ability, were as acceptable to God as those talents, like the widow's two mites that outweighed the rich men's gifts in the sight of the Lord. The threescore and seven garments for the priests, added to the gold and silver, show a people mindful that the ministers of the restored house must be clothed for their service, and giving toward it out of their scanty store.

The witnesses read the verse as the seal of the whole offering. Governor, heads of houses, and common people alike had a part in it, each giving as he was able, so that the rebuilding of the house of God was the work not of a few great men but of the willing nation. Whatever is given to that work, Henry had said, God is not unrighteous to forget; and here the humblest givers, the rest of the people who had neither the governor's rank nor the chief fathers' wealth, are numbered among the benefactors of the temple, their drams recorded with the same care as the greater gifts. The witnesses honour the offering for its universality and its heart: a poor and returning people, out of their poverty, laying up gold and silver and priestly garments toward a house not yet built, that the worship of God might be restored in the place of the ruined altar.
73:
So the priests, and the Levites, and the porters, and the singers, and some of the people, and the Nethinims, and all Israel, dwelt in their cities: the great register closes as the people settle into their places, and the reformed John Gill notes that the cities were those assigned them out of the several tribes, in which they or their forefathers had dwelt before the captivity. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke shows how the enrolment served this very end. It was with reference to this settlement, he says, that the public registers had been examined, for by them the different families were found, and with them the cities and villages that belonged to each by the ancient division of the land; and he marks the very calendar of it, that the wall was finished in the sixth month, Elul (as Nehemiah 6:15 records), Nehemiah then set the examination on foot, and by the seventh month, Tisri, the families had come into their paternal cities. The register determined everything, so that there was no room for complaint, and none could charge the governor with partiality.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears a note of triumph in the closing phrase. The emphasis, he says, lies in the words 'all Israel in their cities,' for though Judah and Benjamin had furnished the greatest part of the returning host, this was no partial affair but a national revival, and the repeated 'in their cities' carries that note. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds the harmony of the settlement, that they dwelt in peace and in perfect unity, a blessed presage of their establishment.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a closing reflection. Their cities were out of repair, he grants, yet because they were their cities, such as God had assigned them, they were content to dwell in them, thankful for liberty and property though they had little of pomp or plenty; here was room enough for them all, so that there was no strife but perfect harmony, a happy presage of their peace. The witnesses read the last verse of the register as the quiet consummation of all that went before. The long roll of names and numbers, families and priests and Levites and given ones, ends not in a heap of statistics but in a people come home, each to his own place, the nation reconstituted city by city upon its old foundations; and Henry turns it to the reader's heart, that those who at the call of the gospel forsake sin and return to the Lord shall likewise be brought safely home at last to the holy city of God, of which this return from Babylon was but a shadow.
7:
At the head of the returning host stand its leaders, and the witnesses read the roll of names with an eye to its parallel. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott had observed that the chiefs were perhaps meant to represent the twelve tribes, given by twelve names, though in the copy at Ezra 2 one of them, Nahamani, has dropped out and three others appear in slightly altered forms. Here in Nehemiah the twelfth name is restored to its place, so that the company is complete: Zerubbabel and Jeshua, then Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, and Baanah, the fuller list confirming what the other had left defective.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains why the two rolls should differ at all. The register Nehemiah found, he says, was that of the persons who came up long before, in the first return under Zerubbabel and Joshua; and such a list could not answer in every point to the state of the people in his own day, for several named in it were by then dead, and others had arrived since. Nehemiah therefore altered it only in part, leaving the body of it as it stood, and this accounts for the variations between it and the register in Ezra. His fellow wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds a like caution about the sums that follow, that the Tirshatha here named is Nehemiah, and that it is no wonder the monies and other gifts differ from those in Ezra 2:68, this being another and later collection than the first.

The elder witnesses fix the chief men themselves. The reformed John Gill takes Jeshua for Joshua the high priest, the son of Josedech, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes Zerubbabel and Jeshua the new Moses and Aaron of the people, their chief prince and their chief priest. Over the other great names a question hangs, whether the Nehemiah and Mordecai here are the famous men who bore those names or merely others of the same; Henry inclines to think them the same, come now and afterward returned to their work, while Gill judges them different men, since the famous Nehemiah came to Jerusalem only in a later reign. The witnesses do not force the point. They agree that the verse names the founders of the second commonwealth, prince and priest at their head and ten more beside, and that the differences from Ezra's copy are the natural marks of a list first drawn in Babylon and renewed, with additions and losses, when the work of rebuilding was well advanced.
8:
With the children of Parosh, two thousand a hundred and seventy-two, the enumeration of the lay families begins, and the witnesses use this first entry to set the rule for reading the whole. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, noting that this chapter is almost entirely the same as the second of Ezra, refers the reader thither for the substance, and there he had laid down the distinction that governs the list: where the word 'children' stands before the name of a man, as here before Parosh, it means his descendants; where it stands before the name of a place, it means the inhabitants of that place. The reader must watch, house by house, whether the head-name is a father or a town.

The reformed John Gill describes the same character in the roll, that from here the returning captives are set down by their families, by the ancestors from whom they sprang or the towns to which they had belonged, and by their numbers, so that of most of them nothing else is now known. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fixes the recurring word to the same sense: the children of Parosh are his posterity, all who descended from him or from the family whereof he was chief, and so for all the rest.

The grammatical-historical witnesses turn to the numbers. Charles Ellicott sets Parosh at the head of a comparison he will pursue name by name through the three authorities, and marks that here at the outset the count agrees in all, two thousand a hundred and seventy-two in this register as in the parallel roll of Ezra 2:3; it is only further on that the copies begin to part. Keil and Delitzsch, setting the families in parallel columns, confirm the agreement, a reminder that the divergences to come are the exceptions in a list largely faithful in both its copies; that Parosh stands at the very figure it bears in the sister roll is itself a small pledge that the document, for all its later variants, was in substance one and the same in both hands. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts even this first line above the counting-house, finding it good that a people so lately restored should remember their small beginnings and acknowledge God in multiplying their families; the genealogies here preserved, he elsewhere notes, were kept up until the Messiah should come, after whom such pedigrees would have their end. The witnesses make of the plain entry a lesson in method and in gratitude at once: Parosh, the largest of the lay houses, stands first, its number sure in every witness, the family named from its ancestor and set at the head of all that follow, the pattern by which every later house is to be read, whether its count agree with the parallel roll or, as many will, diverge from it.
19:
The children of Bigvai, two thousand threescore and seven: and here the register parts from its parallel, for where this text reads two thousand and sixty-seven, the twin roll of Ezra 2:14 gives two thousand fifty and six. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes the small confusion of the copies, that some manuscripts here read two thousand and sixty-six, a figure standing between the two; the difference among the witnesses is of a handful of souls, yet the register is exact enough to record it.

Over such divergences the witnesses offer their standing explanations, and here they genuinely differ. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian, would account for the gap between the two rolls as he accounts for all its like: so many, he supposes, set out from Babylon, but some died on the way or were hindered by sickness and other casualty, so that fewer came at last to Jerusalem; the one figure counts those who marched out, the other those who arrived, and the like may be said of all the similar differences, which it suffices to hint once for all. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, setting the houses in parallel columns, take such variations rather for the ordinary marks of documents copied and recopied by hand, where a figure may easily slip; and Charles Ellicott, weighing the three authorities together, notes on which side the greater weight of the copies falls without forcing a reconciliation. Adam Clarke keeps to his own account, that the three witnesses correct one another and that the surplus of names in one, added to another, brings the reckonings into agreement.

The difference is friendly and the substance untouched; whichever way the gap is explained, the house of Bigvai is a true and considerable company of the return, two thousand strong or thereabouts, its exact tale wavering only by a few between the copies. The witnesses turn the little discrepancy into a lesson in patience with an ancient text, neither hiding the variation nor magnifying it, but setting the readings side by side and letting the honest difference stand. It is worth marking, too, that none of them will make the divergence a stick to beat the record with; a slip of a few souls in a column of thousands, whether owing to the road, the pen, or the two occasions of the count, leaves the substance of the house untouched and the credit of the register whole. Bigvai's sons, whether two thousand sixty-seven at their setting out or two thousand fifty-six at their coming home, are numbered among the returning host; and the very care with which so slight a divergence is preserved is itself a pledge of the fidelity with which the whole long roll was kept and handed down.
33:
The men of the other Nebo, fifty and two: a town rather than a father, and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives close attention to the little word 'other.' It is not found in the parallel place at Ezra 2:29, he observes, where the entry stands simply as the children of Nebo, and it is wanting here as well in many of the manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi; the number, fifty-two, is the same in both rolls. As to the place itself, Clarke supposes this Nebo to be the same as Nob or Nobah, a town in the tribe of Benjamin, so that the entry counts the returning inhabitants of a Benjamite village and not the posterity of any man.

The reading turns, then, on the rule that governs the whole list. By the distinction Clarke had laid down, 'children' or 'men' set before the name of a place means those who dwelt in it; and so the men of Nebo are the remnant of that town, come home to the seats of their fathers. The word 'other,' where the text carries it, serves to distinguish this Nebo from some better-known place of the name, much as the register elsewhere marks a second house against a first; and its absence from Ezra's copy, like so many small differences between the two, the grammatical-historical witnesses take for the ordinary variation of documents long copied by hand, a matter of a single word added or dropped, with the substance untouched.

The reformed John Gill keeps the larger frame, that from the head of the roll to its end the captives are described sometimes by their ancestors and sometimes by the towns in which they or their forefathers had formerly dwelt, and that of most of them nothing more is now known. Nebo belongs to the second sort, a small Benjamite town whose scattered survivors, but fifty-two in all, are here counted home. The witnesses make no legend of so bare an entry; they fix the place, note the disputed word and the agreeing number, and let it stand as one more little company of the return. That so obscure a village, and so slight a band, should be preserved at all, and preserved in copies that can be checked one against another down to a single word, is itself the quiet testimony of the passage, that God kept account of even the least of the towns of his people, and forgot neither the fifty-two of Nebo nor the name of the place they came home to.
34:
The children of the other Elam, a thousand two hundred fifty and four: and the register, having named one house of Elam already, is careful to mark this as a second. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes the purpose of the added word plainly: 'the other Elam' is so called to distinguish this house from the Elam mentioned above at v.12, the two families bearing the one name. What is stranger still, and what the witnesses feel without fully explaining, is that the two houses carry not only the same name but the very same number, a thousand two hundred and fifty-four apiece, so that the register distinguishes by the qualifier 'other' two companies that the figures alone could never have told apart.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, setting the roll in parallel columns, record this second Elam at its thousand two hundred and fifty-four and find it standing at the same figure in the twin list of Ezra 2:31; here, as with the first Elam, the two copies agree. The repetition of the identical number in both houses and in both rolls is one of the small puzzles of the catalogue, which the witnesses record faithfully rather than resolve, unwilling to emend away a reading that the copies concur in preserving.

The reformed John Gill keeps the entry within the character of the whole, one more family described only by the name it bore and the number it counted, of whom nothing else is known; and by the rule the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke had laid down, the word 'children' set before such a personal name marks the descendants of a man and not the dwellers in a town, so that this second Elam, like the first, is a house traced to its father. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry would not have the reader slight so bare a line, for the very repetition of the roll betokens the delight God takes in his people, and his knowledge of them, house by house and name by name. The witnesses read the two Elams together as a lesson in the register's exactness. A less careful record might have merged the two houses into one, or silently dropped the duplicate; but this roll keeps them distinct, calling the second 'other' precisely because it could not otherwise be told from the first, and both copies hand the strange coincidence down unaltered. The children of the second Elam, a thousand two hundred and fifty-four strong, take their place in the muster beside their namesakes, two houses of one name and one number, kept apart in the sacred account by a single distinguishing word, that neither might be lost in the other nor either forgotten in the roll of the returning people.
54:
The children of Bazlith, the children of Mehida, the children of Harsha: three more of the Nethinim, and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke pauses over the middle name to note a divergence of the copies. For the children of Mehida, he observes, many of the manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi read Mehira, the one letter altered between the witnesses; and the parallel roll at Ezra 2:52 carries the same little cluster of names, Bazluth and Mehida and Harsha, with the small differences of spelling that run all through this part of the list.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch gather such entries into their reckoning of the whole class. These are among the thirty-five households of the Nethinim, the temple-bondsmen whose sum, joined with the ten houses of Solomon's servants, came to only three hundred and ninety-two, so that a name like Bazlith or Harsha may stand for no more than a single little family come up from Babylon. Through this stretch, they note, the parallel register now agrees and now diverges, a house present in the one and absent in the other, a name spelled here in one fashion and there in another; and they take these differences for the ordinary marks of a text long copied by hand, to be recorded soberly and left to stand.

The reformed John Gill keeps the reader mindful of what the whole file amounts to, the descendants of the Gibeonites and their fellows, given of old to the service of the sanctuary, of whom nothing now remains but these bare designations in the catalogue of the return. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets over such lowly names his standing word, that it is an honour to belong to God's house, though in the meanest office there; and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley had fixed their calling once for all, as persons devoted to the inferior services of the priests and Levites, in which light even this dry cluster of Bazlith and Mehida and Harsha is to be read. The witnesses make no attempt to trace them further, for nothing more can be traced; they fix the names, note the variant that one of them carries between the copies, and let the entry stand as one more company of the given ones. That the sacred record should spend its lines on names that carry no story and no number of their own, and should preserve them so exactly that even a single altered letter is marked and weighed, is itself the lesson of the verse: in the account God keeps of his house, the wood-carriers and the water-drawers are numbered as carefully as the princes and the priests, and Bazlith and Mehida and Harsha are written down, household by household, for the honour of their service.
68:
Their horses, seven hundred thirty and six; their mules, two hundred forty and five: the register turns to the beasts the returning host brought with them, and the witnesses read the modest count from two sides. The reformed John Gill takes the small number for a mark of the people's poverty: so few horses and mules could carry little more than the goods and baggage, so that the far greater part of the company must have walked home on foot, the horse and the mule being in the East the mounts of the better sort. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same tally the happier way: a people who had gone into captivity stripped of everything now returned from it abounding in substantial riches, seven hundred and thirty-six horses, two hundred and forty-five mules, and, as the following verses add, camels and asses in their hundreds and thousands, besides gold and silver and rich stuffs.

Clarke notes, too, a curiosity of the text, that this whole verse is wanting in fifty of Kennicott's manuscripts and in many of De Rossi's, and in several of the ancient versions, though it stands secure in the parallel place at Ezra 2:66. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the reckoning against that parallel, observing that these numbers, unlike the counts of the men, stand identical in both registers, the two rolls agreeing exactly in the tale of the animals even where they differ over the people.

The two readings, Gill's and Clarke's, are not truly at odds but two sides of one truth. Measured against the wealth of a settled nation, the returning company was poor, its riders few and its walkers many; measured against the destitution in which they had entered Babylon, they came home laden, God having blessed them in the land of their captivity with an increase of substance as well as of numbers. The witnesses let the beasts of burden preach this double lesson, and Keil and Delitzsch's care to note that the horses and mules stand at the same figures in both copies, where the counts of men so often part, is itself a small reassurance, that the inventory of the return was kept with an exactness the discrepancies elsewhere do not overthrow. Seven hundred horses and some hundreds of mules, few for so great a host and yet more than a stripped people might have hoped, bore the substance of the exiles back across the wilderness to their own land.
69:
Their camels, four hundred thirty and five; their asses, six thousand seven hundred and twenty: the tale of the beasts is completed, and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that these numbers, like the horses and mules before them, stand the same in the parallel roll of Ezra 2:67, the two registers agreeing exactly in the reckoning of the animals even where they differ in the reckoning of the men. The camels, few and precious, were the beasts for the long desert stages of the journey; the asses, many times their number, were the common carriers of an ordinary household's goods.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes on that disproportion. The asses, he observes, as throughout the earlier Hebrew history, are the chief and most numerous of the beasts of burden, six thousand seven hundred and twenty of them against a few hundred camels; it is the patient ass, the drudge of the countryside, and not the stately camel, that bears the weight of such a migration. The number tells its own tale of a people not travelling in state but moving house, their possessions loaded on the humble beast of the poor.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps up the note he had struck at the horses, that a people once stripped of everything now returned abounding in substantial riches, their camels and asses counted in the hundreds and thousands. He marks besides a small matter of the text, that after this verse Jerome inserted in the Latin a sentence declaring that thus far the register reached and that what follows belongs to the history of Nehemiah, though the addition stands in neither the Hebrew nor the ancient versions. The witnesses read the closing line of the inventory as both a plain record and a quiet doxology. Plain, because the historian sets down the camels and asses with the same exactness he gave the priests and the singers, and because their number agrees to a beast with the parallel account; a doxology, because the sum of it all shows a company that God had not sent home empty. The exiles who had hung their harps on the willows of Babylon returned with beasts enough to carry their substance across the wilderness, and Ellicott's homely observation, that it was the ass above all that bore the load, only deepens the picture of a humble but not destitute people, plodding back to their land behind the creatures that had always served the households of Israel.
12:
The children of Elam, a thousand two hundred fifty and four: a great lay house, and one of those where the two registers stand at perfect one. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, who set the whole roll of families in parallel columns, record Elam at a thousand two hundred and fifty-four here and the very same in the twin list of Ezra 2:7; here the copies do not part. Charles Ellicott, pursuing his comparison of the three authorities name by name, reckons Elam among the entries on which the witnesses agree, and it is precisely such agreements, he holds, that fix the shape of the document, so that when a later figure varies the reader knows it for a variation.

A curiosity attends the name, which the witnesses do not miss: the same 'children of Elam,' numbered again at a thousand two hundred and fifty-four, will appear a second time further down the list, where v.34 speaks of 'the other Elam.' The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the added word 'other' as meant to distinguish that second house from this first Elam; two families bore the one name and the one number, and the register keeps them apart by the little qualifier. Clarke keeps before the reader, too, his larger reconciliation, that this roll, the roll of Ezra, and the apocryphal Esdras correct one another, so that even where a figure might seem to waver the three copies together preserve the truth.

The reformed John Gill sets Elam among the many houses described only by the ancestor from whom they sprang, of whom nothing more is now known than the name and the number here recorded; and John Wesley, for his part, would have every such head-name read as a father rather than a town, the children of Elam being his posterity, all who descended from him or from the family whereof he was chief. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the dry entry its worth, for the keeping of such an account was an honour to the families that came up and a benefit to their posterity, that they might know from whom they descended and to whom they were allied; the great God, he says, has his eye on the register of the children of the captivity and knows them all by name. The witnesses leave the verse balanced between the critic's note and the believer's comfort: a house of some twelve hundred souls, its number steady in every copy, its name shared with another family that the record is careful to distinguish, and its place kept faithfully in the roll of a people whom God was bringing home.
24:
The children of Hariph, an hundred and twelve: a small house, but one that shows the register's divergences are not of number only but of name. For where this text reads Hariph, the parallel roll of Ezra 2:18 reads the children of Jorah, and yet both agree in the count of a hundred and twelve, so that the two names plainly belong to one and the same family. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley had offered just this as one cause of the differences between the copies, that several names were given to the same persons; and here is a clear instance, a single house called Hariph in the one roll and Jorah in the other, its identity fixed beyond doubt by the number that never changes.

The grammatical-historical witnesses handle it as a matter of the text. Keil and Delitzsch, ranging the families in parallel columns, note where a name in this register answers to a slightly altered or wholly different form in its twin, and take such variations, where the number holds steady, for the ordinary marks of a document long transmitted by hand. Charles Ellicott, comparing the three authorities house by house, marks the same, weighing which form the weight of the copies supports, but never doubting that the differing names cover the one company. The variation touches the shape of the word, not the substance of the list.

The reformed John Gill keeps the character of the whole section in view, that the returning captives are set down sometimes by the ancestor from whom they sprang and sometimes by the town where they had dwelt, and that of most of them nothing survives but what is here recorded; and by the rule the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke had laid down, 'children' before such a personal name means the descendants of the man, not the dwellers in a place. The witnesses make of this obscure entry a small but telling proof of their method: a house whose very name differs between the copies is yet recognised for one, because the register that could vary a name kept the number sure. Hariph, or Jorah, sends home but a hundred and twelve souls, a little company lost among the larger houses; and the care with which both its names are preserved, and both reconciled by its unchanging count, is one more token of the sober fidelity that guarded even the least families of the return.
48:
The children of Lebana, the children of Hagaba, the children of Shalmai: three houses of the Nethinim, set down in the long file of the temple's given ones. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, who number the whole company together, count these among the thirty-five families of temple-bondsmen who, with the ten houses of Solomon's servants, made up in all but three hundred and ninety-two persons, so small were the clans that each averaged only eight or nine souls. They note the textual state of the roll along this stretch, that the name here written Shalmai appears in the parallel of Ezra 2:44 and its neighbours in slightly altered forms, one copy reading Salmai and another Shamlai, while some houses stand in the one register and are wanting in the other; yet these variations, they judge, touch only the shape of the words and not the substance of the list.

The reformed John Gill keeps before the reader what these given ones were. The Nethinim, he holds with the older Jewish teachers, were the Gibeonites, given first by Joshua to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God (Joshua 9:27), and afterward by David to assist the Levites; the very name Nethinim means the given ones. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same, that they were persons devoted to the inferior services of the priests and Levites, and it is in that light he would have even this bare column of Lebana and Hagaba and Shalmai read.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies the sense that redeems the dryness of the verse. It is an honour, he says, to belong to God's house, though in the meanest office there; and these obscure households, whose names would else have perished utterly, are kept in the sacred roll because they and their fathers had given themselves to the lowly work of the sanctuary, the wood and the water without which the altar could not burn. The witnesses read the three little houses as a further proof of the truth the whole roll declares, that God forgets none of his servants, however small their clan or humble their task. Bound to Jerusalem by nothing but their office and their devotion, when they might have stayed in Babylon unmissed, Lebana and Hagaba and Shalmai came up to take again the drudgery of the temple, and the historian numbers them, household by household, that their return might be remembered when all else about them was forgotten.
60:
All the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety and two: the register sums the two lowest orders of the temple's servants in a single total, and the witnesses read the small figure with care. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make the reckoning exact: thirty-five families of the Nethinim and ten houses of Solomon's servants together amounted to but three hundred and ninety-two persons, so that each family can have averaged only eight or nine souls; and the same sum, they note, stands in the parallel roll of Ezra 2:58, the two copies agreeing in the total even where their several names show the small variations of a hand-copied text.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott distinguishes the two classes here joined. The Nethinim were the given ones, devoted of old to the meaner services of the house; the children of Solomon's servants were the class formed, as the history of Solomon tells (1 Kings 9:21), of the remnant of the Canaanites, a servile order probably inferior even to the Nethinim, though generally reckoned with them, as here in the common enumeration. Yet both, he observes, retained through all the captivity their attachment to the service into which they had been received; and the Levites being now so few, their value in the rebuilding of the temple gave them the importance they assume in these books.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds the touch of feeling that clings to the second name, that these had lived in Solomon's household and afterward called themselves and their families by his name, esteeming it a great honour to have served so great a prince; and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets over the whole his rule that it is an honour to belong to God's house though in the meanest office there. The witnesses read the little company of three hundred and ninety-two with a certain tenderness. Sprung, many of them, from a conquered and servile stock, and bound to Jerusalem by nothing but an inherited office, they might have been thought least likely to care for the return; yet they had kept their attachment to the house through all the years of exile, and came up now, when the ministering tribes were thin, to lend their humble labour to the work. That the sacred writer should count the given ones and the servants of Solomon with the same exactness he gives the priests, and that both copies should hand down their total unaltered, is the quiet witness of the verse, that none who loved the sanctuary, however low his birth or mean his task, went unremembered in the roll of the return.
